newsitem.title: USA: CSCE coffee sweeps to 27-month highs, funds buy.
newsitem.headline: CSCE coffee sweeps to 27-month highs, funds buy.

text.p: CSCE coffee prices staged an explosive rally Tuesday as scarce supply propelled the market to its highest level in 27 months, trading sources said.
Prices soared as much as 12 cents at one point, fueled by heavy shortcovering and new buying on the part of commodity funds. Benchmark May futures closed at 195.25 cents a lb, up 10.40 cents.
While no new fundamentals emerged during today's run-up, analysts said a series of recent bullish developments set the stage for the rally.

Among the factors cited were a Merrill Lynch forecast for a surprisingly low crop yield in Colombia, and a suggestion by a USDA official that total world output for the current crop year might be smaller than initially thought.

"You just don't have a plentiful supply of coffee right now," said Smith Barney analyst Walter Spilka. While the market appeared ripe for a pullback after rising 14 percent in the last three days alone, coffee prices may not yet have seen the end of their bull run, he said.
"What the market will do now is correct in the next day or two, and then maybe go up again," Spilka said. "I don't see stocks increasing."

However, he cautioned that higher values should eventually attract more coffee from producing countries into the market, he said. In addition, the sky-high prices threaten to scare off consumers and stall the rally.
U.S. roasters were among today's buyers, while producer-linked selling was thin on the ground, dealers said.
Traders also cited the market's increasingly robust technical stance. Key buy stops were activated today at 190 and 193.50 cents, and 195, triggering sucessive waves of speculative buying, they said.

The market came within striking distance of the widely watched 200.00-cent ($2) mark today, hitting a session high of 199.50 on May futures. Coffee prices last traded above $2 in 1994, when two severe frosts in top-grower Brazil led to sharply depleted world supply. ((-- Wendy Pollack, New York Commodities Desk 212 859 1640))
